name: Suruwaha
catalog_quote: Suruwahá feet are right-headed (iambic) and are oriented from right-to-left. These alignment constraints are stated in (118) and (119): (118) ALIGN FT (FT, R, PRWD, R) (119) ALIGN HD (HD, FT R) ... (121) a. dakùhurú 'to put in the fire' b. tàburí 'vestige/track' c. dànazú 'difficult/dumb' d. hàbanùhurú 'to get away' || in Suruwahá, word-initial vowels are always stressed in words of odd-numbered …

audit.recode_to: Keep classification fixed-strict with final primary stress (both sources agree: Everett's iambs R->L put main stress on the final mora; Suzuki 1997 p.80 'sempre a última sílaba'). Revise the rhythm/rule string, which currently encodes Everett's exhaustive iambic parse alternating stress from the right: Suzuki 1997 pp.81-82 gives 4-syllable words as [ˌσσσˈσ] = 1001 (initial secondary, no stress on syllable 2, with segmental evidence from h/r-syllable reduction), i.e. stress placement coded per word length as 01 101 1001 (1 = a stressed syllable) (1..1)' — a final-primary + initial-secondary (hammock) pattern rather than alternating iambs. At minimum add Suzuki 1997 sec. 4.2 to 'contra' and mark the secondary-stress pattern as disputed between the two primary sources; resolve with Huber Azevedo 2024 when obtained.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Everett 1996 passages are present verbatim at the stated pages in the text we hold/PDF. (2) The classification rests on a 1996 unpublished OT working paper whose Suruwahá data are second-hand (Suzuki tapes); it is a legitimate phonology source but not the only or latest one. (3) I downloaded E. Suzuki 1997 (Unicamp MA, open) and read sec. 4.2 from page images: it confirms obligatory final primary stress (so 'fixed-strict, final' stands) but explicitly argues against Everett's/M. Suzuki's iambic secondary stresses, placing secondary stress always on the first syllable and denying stress on syllable 2 of 4-syllable words ([ˌharakaˈdɨ], [ˌmakahaˈra], [ˌawabiˈdʒa]) — this contradicts the '0101' cell of our rule string.
